Biol. 2023, 12, 3381−3392 ![](images/a832c7e80354c13bab5f69286ac0c471bd5ac61aae7e06255b0a045b47282671.jpg) Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: Isopentyldiol (IPDO) is an important raw material in the cosmetic industry. So far, IPDO is exclusively produced through chemical synthesis. Growing interest in natural personal care products has inspired the quest to develop a biobased process. We previously reported a biosynthetic route that produces IPDO via extending the leucine catabolism (route A), the eficiency of which, however, is not satisfactory. To address this issue, we computationally designed a novel non-natural IPDO synthesis pathway (route B) using RetroPath RL, the state-of-the-art tool for bioretrosynthesis based on artificial intelligence methods. We compared this new pathway with route A and two other intuitively designed routes for IPDO biosynthesis from various perspectives. Route B, which exhibits the highest thermodynamic driving force, least non-native reaction steps, and lowest energy requirements, appeared to hold the greatest potential for IPDO production. All three newly \*sı Supporting Information ![](images/ec1d8cbd7579ea23d403e14fefa6aef9a53ce1d9cd4efa377f98ccfca16abd01.jpg) designed routes were then implemented in the Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) strain. Results show that the computationally designed route B can produce 2.2 mg/L IPDO from glucose but no IPDO production from routes C and D. These results highlight the importance and usefulness of in silico design and comprehensive evaluation of the potential eficiencies of candidate pathways in constructing novel non-natural pathways for the production of biochemicals. KEYWORDS: isopentyldiol, diol, retrosynthesis, pathway evaluation, thermodynamics analysis, synthetic biology ## 1. INTRODUCTION Presently, the majority of value-added compounds, such as solvents, biofuels, and polymer precursors, are produced through petroleum-dependent and energy-intensive chemical processes. Great concerns about climate change, air pollution, and oil price fluctuation have inspired the quest for alternative green processes that produce the desired products with low toxic byproduct formation and carbon dioxide emission. Biobased production processes using renewable feedstocks as substrates hold great potential for a sustainable supply of chemicals. Synthetic biology aims at designing and altering the host metabolic system as well as introducing artificial pathways whose behavior can be predicted, programed, and, finally, controlled.1−3 Short-chain (C3−C5) diols are considered a class of important green platform chemicals that have wide applications in manufacturing a variety of commercial chemical products, such as cosmetics, feed additives, polymers, solvents and pharmaceuticals.4−6 Isopentyldiol (IPDO) is an appealing ingredient in cosmetic industry. It has no odor or irritation and is evaluated as a safe and eco-friendly material. Compared to other diols used in cosmetics (such as propylene glycol, butylene glycol, or dipropylene glycol), IPDO presents better skin feel, and deodorant and antibacterial performances and therefore can work as a moisturizer, solubilizer, and booster of preservatives. Recently, we proposed a general route for microbial production of structurally diverse diols by expanding the amino acid metabolism.7 This general route combines oxidative and reductive formations of the diol hydroxyl groups and comprises four reactions catalyzed by amino acid hydroxylase, L-amino acid deaminase, α-keto acid decarboxylase, and aldehyde reductase consecutively. As a proof of concept, the feasibility of IPDO production via this general route has been verified (named here route A). To increase the IPDO titer, further eforts have been made, including screening for pathway enzymes with higher activity, enhancing the supply of the precursor amino acid, and directed evolution of the key enzyme hydroxylase. The achieved IPDO titer of 310 mg/L is, however, still far from the requirement of a practical application. In view of this, we explore in this study the possibility of producing IPDO via alternative artificial biosynthetic routes. ![](images/2a4ccaea20ab262bde1a652ba4a5e6e93f82f9ae7e03ef829fa470a7e37279d1.jpg) ![](images/88084f2af8ca381a6be1645121cd7563222e0bbb9aeef0cf815c894d4f34e0fc.jpg) Figure 1. Designing an artificial biosynthetic route is a process that generally consists of three steps: (1) design and evaluation of pathways; (2) verification of the designed pathways in vivo or in vitro; and (3) improving the production of target compounds by applying metabolic engineering strategies.2 The development of computational pathway prediction tools has largely facilitated the identification of possible metabolic pathways and the corresponding enzymes. Currently, a number of prediction algorithms have been developed to aid in the biosynthetic route design, such as BNICE.ch,8 RetroPath $\mathrm { R L } , ^ { 9 }$ and Retrobiocat.3 These pathway design tools use the retrosynthetic analysis (RTSA) method, often used in chemical synthesis. RTSA uses a set of reaction rules to backtrack from target products to potential reactants and connect individual reactions to form pathways. A scoring function is then used to rank the generated pathways based on reaction thermodynamic parameters, substrate/product similarity, potential toxicity of intermediates, and the number of enzymes that need to be heterologously expressed so as to select for more rational biosynthetic pathways. The advantage of the RTSA-based pathway design is that the target product is not limited to known natural metabolites of a microbial host but can also be a completely new molecular structure. Moreover, as the technology of enzyme design advances, the diversity of substrates that enzymes can catalyze will broaden, enabling the synthesis of more diverse products using the generalized reaction rules of the retrosynthetic pathway design method. One landmark in the application of computer-aided design in metabolic engineering is the biological production of 1,4- butanediol.10 In their work, more than 10,000 pathways were initially identified using the software Bio-Pathway Predictor, followed by selection using a pathway selection software to sort and rank the pathways based on attributes including maximum theoretical yield, thermodynamic feasibility, number of nonnative reaction steps, and pathway length. As a result, two highranking artificial routes were selected for metabolic engineering, and the best recombinant strain produced 18 g/L 1,4- PDO from glucose after 5 days of cultivation. Prior to the experimental implementation of the three designed routes, we investigated the potential of these designs by using two in silico analysis tools. For comparison, route A serves as the reference route and is evaluated with the other three routes in parallel. We used the flux balance analysis $( \mathrm { F B A } ) ^ { 1 1 }$ to predict the maximum IPDO yield and the max− min driving force $( \mathrm { M D F } ) ^ { 1 2 }$ to determine the pathway thermodynamics so as to predict the feasibility and to identify the key bottlenecks in these pathways. Both tools are wellelucidated and can be easily implemented without the requirement of experimental data, thereby providing a simple and efective means of evaluating diferent artificial pathways that produce the same target compound. Afterward, in comparison with route $\mathbf { A } ,$ all three artificial biosynthetic routes were separately introduced into the Escherichia coli BL21- (DE3) strain, and their performances on IPDO production were analyzed and compared with the in silico prediction results. RESULTS 2.1. Design and Evaluation of the Novel IPDO Biosynthetic Routes. To find a potential retrosynthetic pathway, we used the bioretrosynthesis analysis software Retropath RL to make a computational prediction of the biosynthetic pathway for the target product IPDO. The prediction gave only one reasonable biosynthetic pathway: first, α-KIC was oxidatively decarboxylated by 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase/α-ketoisocaproate dioxygenase (HPD) (EC: 1.13.11.27) to produce 3-OH-IV (Figure 1). 3- OH-IV was then converted to 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanal (3- OH-3-M-BA) by a carboxylic acid reductase (CAR) (EC: 1.2.1.30). Subsequently, 3-OH-3-M-BA was reduced to IPDO by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) (EC: 1.1.1.202). Another pathway was obtained from the second round of selection after modification of the parameters (Figure S1). In this route, 3- OH-IV was obtained by hydrolysis of ethyl 3-hydroxyisovalerate (E-3-OH-IV), which was picked as the starting metabolite of the designed route. However, considering that this precursor is not a natural metabolic intermediate of E. coli but a structure deduced by retrosynthesis, we chose the former pathway for further research. We notice that one distinct structural feature of IPDO is that it contains an isobutyl group, which motivates us to develop novel biosynthesis pathways that generate IPDO from metabolites that share a similar structure. In this regard, we propose two new biosynthetic routes (routes C and D) by selecting $\alpha { , } \beta { \cdot }$ -dihydroxyisovalerate $\left( \alpha , \beta { \mathrm { - D H I V } } \right)$ , an intermediate of the valine biosynthesis pathway, and mevalonate (MVA), respectively, as the precursors for IPDO production. Specifically, in route C, CAR catalyzes the reduction of $\alpha { , } \beta { - }$ DHIV to generate 2,3-dihydroxy-isovaleraldehyde (2,3-diOH-IVA), which in turn is converted to 3-methylbutane-1,2,3-triol (3-M-BTO) by PDDH. 3-M-BTO is transformed to 3-OH-3- M-BA by glycerol dehydratase (GDHt, EC: 4.2.1.30) and subsequently to IPDO by PDDH. In route D, IPDO is produced by stretching the well-elucidated heterologous MVA catabolism.13,14 Specifically, CAR is employed to reduce MVA to 3,5-dihydroxy-3-methylpentanal (3,5-diOH-3-M-PA), which is subsequently converted to IPDO by aldehyde-deformylating oxygenase (ADO) (EC: 4.1.99.5). Unfortunately, the bioretrosynthesis analysis software Retropath RL is unable to forecast routes C and D, even with parameter adjustments. This stems from the rigidity of the rules enforced by Retropath RL concerning the nonreactive atoms neighboring the reaction center. This strict criterion results in the omission of metabolites with similar structures during the path exploration process within Retropath RL. As a result, the algorithm’s capacity to uncover potential nonnatural pathways becomes constrained. Then, to evaluate the potential eficiencies of the four routes, we set several criteria including theoretical yield of IPDO, pathway thermodynamics estimated by the MDF, energy eficiency in form of ATP and NADPH cost, number of nonnative steps, and penalties posed by inappropriate properties of intermediates and pathway enzymes (Table 1). We used FBA to predict their theoretical IPDO yields and corresponding metabolic flux distributions. Results showed that all three proposed IPDO pathways have higher IPDO theoretical yields than that of our previously reported route A (Table 1). The low yield (0.628 mol/mol glucose) of route A is due to the fact that hydroxylation of leucine into 4-OH-Leu in route A is coupled with the oxidation of α-KG to succinate and reduction of the concentration of O to $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } .$ This means that in addition to the carbon loss in the form of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ a certain metabolic flux has to be shunted into α-KG formation to make this coupled reaction feasible, which may impose an “additional burden” for the eficient IPDO production via this route. In contrast, route C starting from $\alpha , \beta \mathrm { - d i O H - I V }$ without carbon loss gives the highest IPDO theoretical yield, reaching 0.827 mol/mol glucose (Table 1 and Figure S2), which is 96.5% of the maximal theoretical yield (0.857 mol/mol glucose) determined purely by the energy balance.15 The theoretical yields of IPDO of routes B reach 0.667 mol/mol glucose. Specifically, one carbon atom is lost as carbon dioxide (CO ) in the oxidative decarboxylation of α-KIC to 3-OH-IV, which reduces its IPDO theoretical yield. As to route D, there are two reactions that involve the carbon loss: one is the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, accompanied by $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ formation, and the other one is the last reaction step of converting 3,5-diOH-3-M-PA to IPDO by ADO, giving rise to a theoretical IPDO yield of 0.667 mol/mol glucose. ![](images/10815936d2132fe593cf2d746c3ec52f023b5e34489bc23a2428850693f917a7.jpg) ![](images/264dff4a053199a60b9870529b97d9c44a82f91c0aa438ef5163f72ac59b07d9.jpg) ![](images/c4b703455749ee67498903e22b7ab3b8b54fee91746306c9c18c844cde9da543.jpg) ![](images/c6d58bf8eb3896b0d1ffdb0940aef064f16ba5ef466120ad62e98b2738945f82.jpg) ![](images/ab215be15487665a893395dfe5001cef303ab0d7d3862a2eb2eda0b1f9f208b4.jpg) ![](images/4700af03d4c6fc71768f0485f0189016ee8e78ed9e9b264ba1a192a843fc50c8.jpg) Figure 2. In addition, the energy eficiencies of the four routes have been calculated. Since all four routes synthesize IPDO via extending pyruvate catabolism, we take pyruvate instead of glucose as the common precursor to recalculate the energy cost of each route. Among them, route A is the most energy eficient route, which only costs 2 molecular NAD(P)H to produce 1 molecular IPDO. Routes B and C exhibit equal energy eficiencies, requiring 2 molecular NAD(P)H in addition to 1 molecular ATP to generate 1 molecular IPDO from pyruvate. The energy eficiency of route C is the lowest, which synthesizes 1 molecular IPDO from pyruvate with the input of 4 and 1 molecular NAD(P)H and ATP, respectively. MDF is used to quantify a pathway’s tendency to operate near-equilibrium and is calculated by setting the minimal driving forces of all reactions as the optimization goal and maximizing $\mathrm { i t . } ^ { 1 2 }$ MDF determines the magnitude of the thermodynamic bottleneck of a given route. In principle, a route with a higher MDF value always means it has a less severe thermodynamic bottleneck and is thermodynamically more favorable. As also shown in Table 1, we determined the MDF values for all four IPDO synthetic routes under the given conditions (Section 4 in the “Materials and $\mathrm { M e t h o d s } ^ { \omega } )$ to evaluate their thermodynamic favorability. Route D with an MDF value of 38.37 kJ/mol seems to be thermodynamically most favorable (Table 1 and Figure 2) among the four routes. However, it has to be noted that its higher MDF value is mainly contributed by the high $\Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime } ~ ( - 9 5 . 1 6 ~ \mathrm { k J / m o l } )$ of the last reaction catalyzed by ADO (Figures 1 and 2), which indicates that all upstream reactions in route D are ratelimiting reactions (Figure 2). This will practically be a problem for the subsequent optimization of this route. Route C gives the lowest MDF value (6.96 kJ/mol), which is mainly attributed to the low $\Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime }$ values of the three reactions catalyzed by CAR (−0.74 kJ/mol), PDDH $\left( - 1 . 2 6 \mathrm { \ k J / m o l } \right)$ and PDDH (−1.26 kJ/mol) consecutively. In comparison, the MDF values of routes A and B are equal to and lower than that of route D. However, since routes A and B also share a thermodynamically clearly unfavorable reaction, that is, the last reaction catalyzed by PDDH $\left( \Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime } \colon - 1 . 2 6 \right)$ kJ/mol, Figures 1 and 2), it seems that their MDF values are severely constrained by this bottleneck reaction. In this way, the contribution of other reactions to the thermodynamic driving forces of the routes is overwhelmingly obscured. To this end, we removed this common bottleneck reaction and recalculated the MDF values of the remaining reactions in routes A and B, which resulted in higher MDF values for both routes (84.67 vs 74.93 kJ/mol). Moreover, the resulting cumulative $\Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime }$ values in routes A and B demonstrate a nearly linear decrease with each added reaction. The thermodynamically highly favorable reactions of hydroxylation, deamination, and decarboxylation in route A and the oxidative decarboxylation reaction in route B provide the powerful push needed for the thermodynami cally unfavorable reduction formation of the hydroxyl group in the last step. The properties of intermediates and enzymes should also be taken into consideration to evaluate the potential of nonnatural biosynthetic pathways. In many artificial biosynthetic pathways, some metabolites are produced as the outcome of the promiscuous activity of heterologous enzymes. The physiochemical properties of these metabolites may restrict the structure of the pathway and ultimately constrain the product yield. Major physiochemical properties of intermediates to be considered include toxicity, stability, and permeability.16 In addition to high catalytic activity and specificity toward the target substrate, an ideal enzyme with industrial application prospects would have a clearly known catalytic mechanism, is easy and cheap to prepare and use, and is resistant to fluctuating cultivation environments (temperature, pH, etc.). Accordingly, we checked the intermediates and enzymes involved in the four IPDO routes and regarded the unfavorable intermediates and enzymes in these four routes as “penalties”. In this regard, α-KIC and $\alpha , \beta { \mathrm { - D H I V } } ,$ , which are intermediates in routes B and $\mathrm { C } ,$ respectively, exhibit lower afinity to HPD and CAR, respectively, compared to the endogenous enzymes that catalyze them, which makes it challenge to rewire the flux from the branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis pathways into the designed IPDO synthetic routes (Table 1). In addition, GDHt employed in route C requires the expensive vitamin ${ \bf B } _ { 1 2 }$ as a cofactor to maintain its activity, which may largely limit its industrial application. The catalytic mechanism of aldehyde-deformylating oxygenase ADO in route D is still controversial,17−20 making its subsequent rational engineering for further improvement of its activity challenging. The drawbacks of GDHt and ADO reduce the implementation priority of route C and route D. Overall, we came up with three new IPDO biosynthetic routes and compared their potential eficiencies with our previously reported route A. All three new routes show higher theoretical IPDO yields than that of route $\mathbf { A } ,$ implying greater potential from a glucose utilization perspective. Routes A and $\mathbf { B } ,$ which produce IPDO by combing oxidative and reductive pathways of −OH group formation, require fewer reducing powers and exhibit higher thermodynamic driving force (as shown by their higher MDF values and bottleneck reactions determined by MDF) than routes C and D that generate both hydroxyl groups of IPDO through the reductive pathway. In addition, route B gives the fewest non-native reaction steps among all four IPDO routes. Unlike routes C and D, route B does not employ enzymes whose activities are conditiondependent or not well-characterized. All of these advantages highlight the priority of route B. In the follow-up study, we conducted the implementation of all three newly proposed IPDO biosynthetic routes in E. coli so as to explore the efectiveness of the methods and criteria used in this study for a priori in silico estimation of the thermodynamic feasibility of designed pathways for a given product and the relative likelihood of alternative reactions. ## 3. IMPLEMENTATION OF THE DESIGNED IPDO BIOSYNTHESIS ROUTES IN E. COLI 3.1. Route B. As illustrated in Figure 1, route B is designed to synthesize IPDO via extension of α-KIC catabolism. HPD catalyzes the transformation of α-KIC to 3-OH-IV, which is subsequently reduced to IPDO under the catalysis of CAR and PDDH, respectively. For the implementation, we began with the verification of the second step in route B, that is, the conversion of 3-OH-IV to 3-OH-3-M-BA catalyzed by CAR. This is because CAR has a wide scope of substrates due to its high promiscuous activity on non-native substrates.21 To this end, CAR from Nocardia iowensis was selected as the first candidate because of its wide scope of substrates.21 In addition, it has been reported that the 4′-phosphopantetheinyl transferases Sfp from Bacillus subtilis can catalyze post-translational modification of CAR by linking phosphopantetheine to the conserved serine of CAR to obtain a fully functional $\mathrm { C A R } ^ { 2 2 }$ Both the car and sfp genes were synthesized and inserted into pCDFDuet, a vector that is designed for the coexpression of two target genes driven by the T7 promoter, generating thereby the plasmid pCDF-car-sfp. The latter was transformed into the E. coli BL21(DE3) strain to obtain a recombinant strain named IPB01 for the subsequent expression and purification of CAR. The results indicate that coexpression of CAR and Sfp is crucial for enhancing the activity of CAR (Table S3), which is in accordance with the previous study.22 For the enzyme activity assay of CAR on 3-OH-IV, benzoic acid (BA), the native substrate of CAR, was used as the positive control. As illustrated in Figure 3a, CAR showed activity on 3-OH-IV, although the activity was more 10 times lower than that on BA (0.045 vs 0.511 μmol/min/mg). Next, the feasibility of IPDO production from 3-OH-IV was verified both in vitro and in vivo. For the in vitro assay, the reaction was performed in HEPES bufer (pH 7.5) containing 0 or 20 mM 3-OH-IV, 10 mM NADPH, 2 mM ATP, 10 mM $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ , 400 μg of CAR, and 200 μg of either the ADH YqhD from E. coli or the methylglyoxal reductase GRE2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain S288c. The reaction was incubated at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 6 h. As shown in Figure 3b, 187.2 and 200.0 mg/L (nearly 2 mM) IPDO were formed from 3- OH-IV by the reactions containing YqhD or GRE2, respectively, while no IPDO was detected in the absence of 3-OH-IV. The higher IPDO titer of the reaction system employing GRE2 demonstrates that the exogenous GRE2 showed an even slightly higher activity on 3-OH-IV than the endogenous YqhD. Given that the amount of IPDO generated was close to the amount of ATP present in the reaction system, it is reasonable to claim that little intermediate 3-OH-3-M-BA was accumulated, and the conversion of 3-OH-IV to 3-OH-3- M-BA by YqhD or GRE2 was very eficient. To verify the feasibility of IPDO production from 3-OH-IV in vivo, we ligated GRE2 into pET28a to obtain pET-gre and cotransformed pET-gre and pCDF-car-sfp into E. coli BL21- (DE3). The recombinant strain named IPB02 was inoculated into 5 mL of LB medium and grown overnight. The overnight culture was then inoculated into 10 mL of FM-II medium with an initial OD of 0.1 with or without the addition of 50 mM 3- OH-IV. 0.1 mM IPTG was added after $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ reached 0.4−0.6. The results showed that 480.0 mg/L IPDO was produced by IPB02 when 50 mM 3-OH-IV was supplemented in the medium, whereas no IPDO was detected in the absence of 3- OH-IV under the same conditions (Figure 3c). Next, the synthesis of IPDO from α-KIC was verified experimentally. We used whole-cell catalysis to convert α-KIC into 3-OH-IV, as described in Section 7 of the Materials and Methods part. DISCUSSION In this study, we have designed three new IPDO biosynthesis pathways in addition to the biosynthetic route (named route A in this study) we reported before.7 Among the three new routes, route B was computationally designed using Retropath RL and also successfully verified in E. coli, while no production of IPDO could be achieved via the two intuitively designed routes C and D. The feasibility of a synthetic pathway is controlled by many constraints, among which thermodynamics, kinetics, and regulation of the enzymes involved and physiochemical properties of metabolites (intermediates and products) and enzymes play predominant roles. In many artificial pathways, some non-natural intermediates are generated due to the promiscuity of the employed pathway enzymes, which makes it dificult to evaluate the physiochemical properties of these metabolites. The enzyme kinetic properties are always laborious and time-consuming to determine and often vary depending on the test conditions as well as on their origins, which largely limits their applications for describing the control that enzyme kinetics exerts on metabolic fluxes. As an alternative, thermodynamic analysis can be performed without using enzyme kinetic parameters and is not dependent on a particular initial steady state.12 Here, taking route A as a reference route, we compared the four designed IPDO routes from the perspective of thermodynamic potential in order to better understand the implementation results. As mentioned above, the hydroxyl group can be obtained through either oxidation of an alkyl group (named the oxidation pathway) or reduction of a carboxyl group to a carbonyl group and then to a hydroxyl group (named the reduction pathway). The reactions that catalyze the formation of hydroxyl groups through an oxidation pathway are thermodynamically favorable since they are often coupled with other exergonic reactions. For instance, hydroxylation of α-KIC by oxygenase HPD in route B couples the oxidation of α-KIC with its decarboxylation, and hydroxylation of leucine by MFL in route A couples with the oxidation of α-KG to succinate. However, the high energetics of these reactions $\left( \Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime } \colon - 1 0 0 \ t \mathrm { o } - 1 2 0 \ \mathrm { k c a l / m o l } \right)$ comes at the expense of one carbon unit loss, which leads to the low theoretical yields of IPDO in routes A and B (Table 1). Nonetheless, Δ G′-dependent thermodynamic analysis is not always decisive. For example, inorganic pyrophosphatase is a specific catalyst for the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate into orthophosphate. In this study, CAR is employed in routes $\mathrm { { B } , C , }$ and D to catalyze the reduction of the carboxylic acid to the corresponding aldehyde using NADPH as the electron donor, accompanied by the formation of diphosphate (PPi) (Figure 1). The subsequent hydrolysis of PPi provides a substantia additional thermodynamic driving force, thus making such reactions functionally irreversible.25 However, the $\Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime 0 }$ value of PPi hydrolysis is surprisingly positive (4.15 kcal/mol, data from MetaCyc EC 3.6.1.1), which means that the whole reaction is even thermodynamically unfavorable when the subsequent PPi hydrolysis is taken into consideration. We infer that this is mainly attributed to the diferences in defined “standard conditions” and physiological environments. In contrast to standard conditions, a previous study revealed that the $\Delta _ { \mathrm { r } } G ^ { \prime 0 }$ value of the hydrolysis of PPi reaction was estimated to be −16.74 kJ/mol under simulated physiological conditions of pH and ionic strength, where the concentrations of Pi and PPi were 2.42 mM and $6 . 2 \ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ respectively.26 The authors further concluded that the hydrolysis of the PPi reaction did not attain equilibrium in vivo. Therefore, it is unwise to merely use standard Gibson free energies of a reaction to simulate its thermodynamic driving force of cells under physiological states, especially when the working condition of a specific enzyme is vastly diferent from the defined “standard conditions. In addition to thermodynamic analysis, enzyme kinetics also plays a significant role in evaluating the feasibilities of artificial routes. Previous research studies reported that CARs have a broad substrate scope, which ranges from aliphatic acids to aromatic, polycyclic, and heterocyclic acids.27 Although CARs attract significant interest, CARs only exhibit substantial reductase activity against substrates whose second functional group is separated from the carboxylate by at least three carbons,28 which largely limit their applications in the biosynthesis field. Apparently, the intermediates $\alpha , \beta { \mathrm { - D H I V } }$ and MVA in routes C and D do not belong to CAR-preferred substrates, and therefore CAR exhibits poor catalytic activities on $\alpha , \beta { \mathrm { - D H I V } }$ and MVA, which is one of the key reasons that leads to the failure of implementation of routes C and D. Therefore, great importance should also be attached to the substrate preferences of the enzymes employed. Comparing the implementation results of the four designed pathways in $\bar { E . }$ coli, we infer that because of the high thermodynamic driving forces and enzymatic activities of routes A and $\mathrm { B } ,$ a significant amount of metabolic flux is channeled to the IPDO synthesis pathway even at low concentrations of the precursors. In contrast, the failed implementation of routes C and D is mainly attributed to the poor kinetics of the reactions catalyzed by CAR. These results underline the significance of performing a priori thermodynamic and kinetic analysis to evaluate diferent biosynthetic pathways that produce the same product. In addition, the eficiencies of the artificial pathways are influenced by the intrinsic environment of the host strain’s intrinsic environment. These non-natural pathways are designed to synthesize target products by rewiring carbon flux from the inherent metabolisms in a competitive manner; therefore, the afinity and activity of the enzymes employed in a heterologous pathway for precursor intermediates are crucial for its eficiency. For instance, in route B, α-KIC is the precursor for IPDO biosynthesis. In the wild-type E. coli strain, the majority of the endogenous α-KIC pool is converted to leucine, which is catalyzed by the branched-chain-amino-acid transaminase IlvE at high eficiency $\left( K _ { \mathrm { m } } \colon 0 . 0 8 \right.$ mM, $K _ { \mathrm { { c a t } } } \mathrm { { : } }$ 24.7 $\mathsf { s } ^ { - 1 } ) . \mathsf { \Sigma } ^ { 2 9 }$ In contrast, the catalytic ability of HPD on α-KIC is much lower $\left( K _ { \mathrm { m } } \colon 0 . 3 2 \right.$ mM, $\dot { K } _ { \mathrm { c a t } } : 6 . 5 \operatorname * { m i n } ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { 3 0 }$ than that of IlvE. Given this, it is less eficient to use HPD to divert the endogenous α-KIC from the leucine synthesis pathway into the IPDO synthesis pathway (Table 1). This is also the case for route $\mathrm { C } ,$ in which CAR competes with endogenous dihydroxyacid dehydratase IlvD for binding the substrate $\alpha , \beta { \mathrm { - D H I V } }$ for IPDO synthesis (Table 1). To further improve the eficiency of route B in future work, on one hand, the importance of improving α-ketoisocaproate dioxygenase that exhibits improved activity on α-KIC, which can be achieved through either rational protein engineering or screening its homologues from diferent species, should be highlighted. On the other hand, a dynamic regulation system can be employed to dynamically control the expression abundance of IlvE. Recently, Hou et al. constructed a bifunctional molecular switch system by using growth phase-dependent promoters and degrons.31 Within their system, dynamic regulation of the expression of IlvE in diferent growth phases can be fulfilled: a high expression level is kept at the exponential growth phase to ensure good cell growth but turned down to a relatively low level when cells reach the stationary phase to avoid shunting metabolic flux toward valine and leucine synthesis. In addition, a series of promoters with diferent strengths and induction phases have been characterized in their toolbox, which can be adopted in our future study for fine-tuning IlvE expression to maximize IPDO production. ## 5.
